title and abstract.summary: The study quantified the relative contribution of honeybees and wild bees to the pollination of apple orchards by examining three functional traits: body size, pollen load purity, and flower handling behavior. It found that flower handling behavior and abundance were the only traits significantly predicting seed set, and that wild bees contributed more to seed set than honeybees in the surveyed apple orchards.

introduction.summary: The study investigates functional traits of wild bees (including flower handling, body size, and pollen composition) to predict seed set in apple orchards, and then uses these traits to estimate the relative pollination services provided by wild bees compared to honeybees at a regional scale in NY. The study measured the contribution of wild bees to seed set in NY apple orchards, comparing their effectiveness to honeybees across the surveyed apple orchards.

methods.summary: The study measured the summed contribution to seed set of the entire wild bee community relative to that of the honeybee in NY apple orchards by using functional traits as a proxy for per-visit effectiveness and multiplying these trait values by the abundance of the bees for each species. The study measured the relative pollinator contribution across apple orchards by analyzing functional traits and abundance data from wild bee communities, which were grouped based on taxonomic relatedness and similar size and behavior patterns.
